entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Exod.39.1-Exod.39.31">Exo 39:1-31</reference> <hi type="italic">Preparation of the priests’ clothes</hi>. - Previous to the description of the dress itself, we have a statement in <reference osisRef="Exod.39.1">Exo 39:1</reference> of the materials employed, and the purpose to which they were devoted (“cloths of service,” see at <reference osisRef="Exod.31.10">Exo 31:10</reference>). The robes consisted of the <hi type="italic">ephod</hi> (<reference osisRef="Exod.39.2-Exod.39.7">Exo 39:2-7</reference>, as in <reference osisRef="Exod.28.6-Exod.28.12">Exo 28:6-12</reference>), the <hi type="italic">choshen</hi> or breastplate (<reference osisRef="Exod.39.8-Exod.39.21">Exo 39:8-21</reference>, as in <reference osisRef="Exod.28.15-Exod.28.29">Exo 28:15-29</reference>), the <hi type="italic">meïl</hi> or over-coat (<reference osisRef="Exod.39.22-Exod.39.26">Exo 39:22-26</reference>, as in <reference osisRef="Exod.28.31-Exod.28.34">Exo 28:31-34</reference>); the <hi type="italic">body-coats, turbans, drawers, and girdles,</hi> for Aaron and his sons (<reference osisRef="Exod.39.27-Exod.39.29">Exo 39:27-29</reference>, as in <reference osisRef="Exod.28.39-Exod.28.40">Exo 28:39-40</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Exod.28.42">Exo 28:42</reference>). The Urim and Thummim are not mentioned (cf. <reference osisRef="Exod.28.30">Exo 28:30</reference>). The head-dresses of the ordinary priests, which are simply called “bonnets” in <reference osisRef="Exod.28.40">Exo 28:40</reference>, are called “goodly bonnets” or “ornamental caps” in <reference osisRef="Exod.39.28">Exo 39:28</reference> of this chapter (מגבּעת פּארי, from פּאר an ornament, cf. פּאר <hi type="italic">ornatus fuit</hi>). The singular, “<hi type="italic">girdle</hi>,” in <reference osisRef="Exod.39.29">Exo 39:29</reference>, with the definite article, “<hi type="italic">the girdle,</hi>” might appear to refer simply to Aaron’s girdle, i.e., the girdle of the high priest; but as there is no special description of the girdles of Aaron’s sons (the ordinary priests) in <reference osisRef="Exod.29.40">Exo 29:40</reference>, where they are distinctly mentioned and called by the same name (<hi type="italic">abnet</hi>) as the girdle of Aaron himself, we can only conclude that they were of the same materials and the same form and make as the latter, and that the singular, האבנט, is used here either in the most general manner, or as a generic noun in a collective sense (see <hi type="italic">Ges.</hi> §109, 1). The last thing mentioned is the diadem upon Aaron’s turban (<reference osisRef="Exod.39.30">Exo 39:30</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.39.31">Exo 39:31</reference>, as in <reference osisRef="Exod.28.36-Exod.28.38">Exo 28:36-38</reference>), so that the order in which the priests’ robes are given here is analogous to the position in which the ark of the covenant and the golden altar stand to one another in the directions concerning the sacred things in ch. 25-30. “For just as all the other things are there placed between the holy ark and the golden altar as the two poles, so here all the rest of the priests’ robes are included between the shoulder-dress, the principal part of the official robes of the high priest, and the golden frontlet, the inscription upon which rendered it the most striking sign of the dignity of his office” (<hi type="italic">Baumgarten</hi>).
entries.content_plain: Exo 39:1-31 Preparation of the priests’ clothes. - Previous to the description of the dress itself, we have a statement in Exo 39:1 of the materials employed, and the purpose to which they were devoted (“cloths of service,” see at Exo 31:10). The robes consisted of the ephod (Exo 39:2-7, as in Exo 28:6-12), the choshen or breastplate (Exo 39:8-21, as in Exo 28:15-29), the meïl or over-coat (Exo 39:22-26, as in Exo 28:31-34); the body-coats, turbans, drawers, and girdles, for Aaron and his sons (Exo 39:27-29, as in Exo 28:39-40, and Exo 28:42). The Urim and Thummim are not mentioned (cf. Exo 28:30). The head-dresses of the ordinary priests, which are simply called “bonnets” in Exo 28:40, are called “goodly bonnets” or “ornamental caps” in Exo 39:28 of this chapter (מגבּעת פּארי, from פּאר an ornament, cf. פּאר ornatus fuit). The singular, “girdle,” in Exo 39:29, with the definite article, “the girdle,” might appear to refer simply to Aaron’s girdle, i.e., the girdle of the high priest; but as there is no special description of the girdles of Aaron’s sons (the ordinary priests) in Exo 29:40, where they are distinctly mentioned and called by the same name (abnet) as the girdle of Aaron himself, we can only conclude that they were of the same materials and the same form and make as the latter, and that the singular, האבנט, is used here either in the most general manner, or as a generic noun in a collective sense (see Ges. §109, 1). The last thing mentioned is the diadem upon Aaron’s turban (Exo 39:30, Exo 39:31, as in Exo 28:36-38), so that the order in which the priests’ robes are given here is analogous to the position in which the ark of the covenant and the golden altar stand to one another in the directions concerning the sacred things in ch. 25-30. “For just as all the other things are there placed between the holy ark and the golden altar as the two poles, so here all the rest of the priests’ robes are included between the shoulder-dress, the principal part of the official robes of the high priest, and the golden frontlet, the inscription upon which rendered it the most striking sign of the dignity of his office” (Baumgarten).

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Exod.39.32-Exod.39.36">Exo 39:32-36</reference> <hi type="italic">Delivery of the work to Moses</hi>. - The different things are again mentioned one by one. By “the tent,” in <reference osisRef="Exod.39.33">Exo 39:33</reference>, we are to understand the two tent-cloths, the one of purple and the other of goats’ hair, by which the <hi type="italic">dwelling</hi> (משׁכּן, generally rendered tabernacle) was made into a tent (אלה). From this it is perfectly obvious, that the variegated cloth formed the inner walls of the dwelling, or covered the boards on the inner side, and that the goats’ hair-cloth formed the other covering. Moreover it is also obvious, that this is the way in which האהל is to be understood, from the fact, that in the list of the things belonging to the ohel the first to be mentioned are the gold and copper hooks (<reference osisRef="Exod.26.6">Exo 26:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.26.11">Exo 26:11</reference>) with which the two halves of the drapery that formed the tent were joined together, and then after that the boards, bolts, pillars, and sockets, as though subordinate to the tent-cloths, and only intended to answer the purpose of spreading them out into a tent of dwelling.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Exod.39.37-Exod.39.39">Exo 39:37-39</reference> <div eID="gen1128" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1129" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">The lamps of the order,</hi>” i.e., the lamps set in order upon the candlestick. In addition to all the vessels of the sanctuary, shew-bread (<reference osisRef="Exod.39.36">Exo 39:36</reference>), holy oil for the candlestick and for anointing, and fragrant incense (<reference osisRef="Exod.39.38">Exo 39:38</reference>), were also prepared and delivered to Moses, - everything, therefore, that was required for the institution of the daily worship, as soon as the tabernacle was set up.
entries.content_plain:
Exo 39:37-39 
 
 “The lamps of the order,” i.e., the lamps set in order upon the candlestick. In addition to all the vessels of the sanctuary, shew-bread (Exo 39:36), holy oil for the candlestick and for anointing, and fragrant incense (Exo 39:38), were also prepared and delivered to Moses, - everything, therefore, that was required for the institution of the daily worship, as soon as the tabernacle was set up.

<reference osisRef="Exod.39.43">Exo 39:43</reference> <div eID="gen1130" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1131" type="x-p"/> When Moses had received and examined all the different articles, and found that everything was made according to the directions of Jehovah, he blessed the children of Israel. The readiness and liberality with which the people had presented the gifts required for this work, and the zeal which they had shown in executing the whole of the work in rather less than half a year (see at <reference osisRef="Exod.40.17">Exo 40:17</reference>), were most cheering signs of the willingness of the Israelites to serve the Lord, for which they could not fail to receive the blessing of God.
